## Household Debt Crisis Ahead

The Bank of Korea's anticipated rate increases of three to four times this year are raising alarm bells for vulnerable borrowers. Those who engaged in aggressive leverage borrowing, commonly known as "young-leveraged" and "debt-investment" borrowers, face sharply increased interest burdens on both mortgage and consumer loans. Economists warn that young renters and actual homeowner-occupants could face an "interest bomb," with particular concerns about the risk of household debt accumulation. The government is now under pressure to conduct thorough risk assessments of household debt exposure as rate hikes loom on the horizon.

## Real Estate Overhaul Planned

Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yoon-cheol confirmed that the government is preparing comprehensive real estate discussions and tax reform initiatives scheduled for later this month. The administration is prioritizing visible results from announced policies with seamless implementation of follow-up measures. Notably, the presidential office is considering a reassessment of taxable standards for ultra-premium single-unit homes, potentially targeting properties exceeding 4 billion won. The benchmark criteria will be clarified when the tax reform plan is released by month's end, with government officials signaling strengthened holding taxes for ultra-high-value properties even for owner-occupants.

## Premium Seoul Housing Crisis

Seoul's top 1% apartment entry price has soared to approximately 4.65 billion won, according to real estate platform Zigbang's first-half analysis. This represents a stark regional disparity, with Gyeonggi province's threshold at 1.85 billion won and Daegu at 1.58 billion won—creating disparities as wide as nine times. As the government plans differential holding tax burdens on ultra-premium homes, market participants closely monitor where the threshold will be set. The premium segment faces particular scrutiny as policy frameworks take shape.

## Panic Buying Grips Seoul Housing Market

Seoul's housing market is experiencing concerning "panic buying" symptoms among some actual homeowners as supply concerns intensify. The capital's apartment supply is expected to drop nearly 50% year-over-year this year, while deposit lease prices have surged at their fastest pace since the 2015 "jeonse crisis" over a decade ago. This twin pressure—plummeting supply and soaring rental prices—is driving purchase conversions, with some units already breaking through peak prices from the 2020-2021 surge period. The vicious cycle of scarce rental inventory and rapid price appreciation is accelerating buyer inflows into the sales market, particularly in popular neighborhoods.

## KOSPI Plummets on Geopolitical Tensions

South Korea's stock market suffered a sharp 4.46% decline, with the KOSPI closing at 6,516.27, dragged down by escalating Middle East tensions and semiconductor peak concerns. The KOSDAQ fell 5.33% to 749.64, approaching levels last seen when President Lee Jae-myung took office in June 2025 at 750.21. Samsung Electronics dropped 4.31% and SK Hynix fell 4.23% as chip concerns persist. Oil price surges to over 90 dollars per barrel intensified inflationary pressures, weighing heavily on investor sentiment. Despite government efforts on July 16th to address leverage ETF volatility through supplementary measures, subsequent trading volumes have only slightly increased.

## Banking Stocks Gain Amid Rate Expectations

In sharp contrast to the broader market's 20.19% decline, banking stocks posted strong gains, with the bank sector rallying significantly. The three-and-a-half-year rate increase serves as a revaluation catalyst, as funds shift from semiconductor concentration toward dividend and value stocks. This divergence reflects market expectations that financial institutions will benefit from higher net interest margins as the BOK tightens monetary policy over the coming months.

## International Tariff Tensions Mount

The Trump administration's 10% global tariff expires in 24 days, with Section 301 tariffs on structural overcapacity and forced labor products imminent. South Korea has been designated under both categories, facing potential 10% to 12.5% tariffs for forced labor concerns following public hearings last month. Concurrently, the administration is implementing selective tariff reductions—cutting aluminum import tariffs by 50% for companies building new or expanding U.S. manufacturing facilities. These trade policy adjustments create opportunities for companies that localize production while increasing headwinds for traditional exporters.

## K-AI Export Initiative Launched

The government is spearheading a "K-AI Package" strategy to support developing nations through integrated artificial intelligence solutions, data centers, and renewable energy infrastructure. This development assistance approach simultaneously bolsters domestic AI, data center, and energy companies' overseas expansion. Deputy Prime Minister Koo outlined the strategy at an external economic ministers' conference, positioning Korean technology as a competitive advantage in emerging markets while addressing global development needs.

## Naver Pursues Trillion-Won AI Investment

Naver Chairman Lee Hae-jin and CEO Choi Soo-yeon are visiting Brookfield's Toronto headquarters this week to discuss billion-dollar AI factory funding structures. The delegation includes CFO Kim Hee-chul and key subsidiary executives, signaling serious negotiations over specific investment frameworks and scale. Naver's planned 1-gigawatt AI data center combines GPU servers, data centers, and power-cooling infrastructure with advanced AI models and cloud technology—representing a critical shift from model development to computational infrastructure competition.

## AI Framework Law Implementation Underway

South Korea's revised AI Basic Law takes effect today, completing the legal infrastructure for industry operations. The amendments establish government and local authority provisions to support vulnerable populations—including disabled persons and elderly citizens—and economically disadvantaged groups lacking AI product access. These legal foundations enable the domestic AI sector to operate within a comprehensive regulatory framework, addressing equity concerns while promoting innovation and competitive growth.

For investors, today's market volatility presents both challenges and opportunities. The household debt situation demands careful portfolio assessment, particularly for leveraged positions. Banking stocks offer attractive valuations given anticipated rate increases, while geopolitical risks warrant cautious semiconductor exposure. The government's real estate reforms could reshape property valuations, making patience advisable pending the month-end tax reform announcement. International tariff uncertainties require monitoring for export-dependent companies, though K-AI and technology infrastructure investments represent longer-term growth opportunities as the government prioritizes industrial advancement.
headline: Bank of Korea Rate Hike Looms Amid Market Turmoil and Household Debt Concerns
